text.title: WebSocket Design Core Rules
text.summary: 10 testable rules grounding the websocket-design methodology. Each rule pairs a binary check with sourced rationale; the final rule is the skip-this-methodology gate referenced by the decision tree.

rule.statement: Every WebSocket message uses a versioned envelope {v, type, channel, id, seq, ts, payload}. Bump v for breaking protocol changes; clients dedupe by seq across reconnects and retry idempotently by id. Raw payloads with no envelope are forbidden.

rationale.source: Internal — WS protocol audits + WS-protocol retros

rule.rationale: Without a versioned envelope you cannot roll out protocol changes gradually; without seq, clients cannot detect duplicates after reconnect; without a per-message id, a retry after an unacknowledged send is indistinguishable from a new message.

rule.statement: Client sends ping every 25–30 seconds; the server disconnects after 2 missed pongs (≈90 s). Application-layer ping/pong is mandatory — TCP keep-alive alone does not satisfy this rule.

rationale.source: MDN WebSocket docs + RFC 6455 + production NAT incidents

rule.rationale: Without heartbeats, stale connections accumulate silently; NAT gateways, corporate firewalls and load balancers close idle TCP connections without RST after 1–5 minutes, leaving the server with zombie sockets and the client believing it is connected. TCP keep-alive defaults are far too slow to catch it.

rule.statement: Every message type has a JSON schema, and the payload is validated against that schema on both the server and the client. Lax or absent validation is forbidden.

rationale.source: JSON Schema usage + production fuzz retros

rule.rationale: Without per-type validation a malformed or hostile payload reaches the handler directly; agents and malicious clients crash handlers with fields the code never anticipated.

rule.statement: Every close emits an RFC 6455 code that truthfully describes the reason: 1000 normal, 1001 going away, 1008 policy violation, 1009 message too big, 4xxx for application-specific reasons. A bare close with no code is forbidden.
rule.rationale: The close code is the only signal the client has to decide reconnect versus give up; without it every disconnect looks identical and the failure cannot be debugged from the client side.

rule.statement: Reconnect with exponential backoff and full jitter: delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^n)); cap the maximum attempt count.

rationale.source: AWS — Exponential Backoff and Jitter (Marc Brooker)

rule.rationale: Reconnect without jitter causes thundering herds: all clients reconnect simultaneously after a deploy, DoSing the auth endpoint.

rule.statement: Authenticate at HTTP upgrade via a short-lived ticket or signed cookie. Never put a long-lived JWT in a query string.
rule.rationale: Query strings appear in server and proxy access logs; a session JWT in logs is an immediate credential leak.

rule.statement: The handshake credential is a signed token with a TTL of at most 5 minutes, single-use, carried in the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header where the client can set it and in the query string only when it cannot. A long-lived cookie as the sole credential is forbidden.
rule.rationale: This bounds what auth-on-upgrade permits: a long-lived cookie cannot be revoked promptly and a stolen one grants indefinite access, while a 5-minute single-use ticket collapses the replay window even if it does reach an access log.

rule.statement: Horizontal scaling requires a Redis Pub/Sub (or NATS) fan-out bus. Each server node subscribes and delivers to its locally connected clients.
rule.rationale: Sockets are pinned to one process; without a shared pubsub bus, a message published on node A never reaches clients connected to node B.

rule.statement: Buffer outbound messages in a bounded per-connection queue with an explicitly declared shed policy — drop_oldest, drop_newest, or close with code 1008. Size it to the memory budget (≈100 for an interactive client, up to ~1000 for a server fan-out queue). Unbounded queues are forbidden.

rationale.source: Internal — backpressure incidents + WebSocket OOM retros

rule.rationale: Unbounded queues accumulate during outages and behind one slow reader; the server OOMs while every health check still reports green, and on reconnect the client floods the server with stale messages. Naming the shed policy is what makes the data loss a decision rather than an accident.

rule.statement: If the workload is one-shot CRUD or server-only push or runs in pure serverless without a stateful tier, skip this methodology and use REST or SSE.
rule.rationale: WebSocket operational cost (heartbeat, reconnect, fan-out) is wasted when REST or SSE meets the latency budget.
